summary: Seaside sits on the Monterey Peninsula but catches almost none of the tourist traffic — visitors blow right past on Highway 1 toward Cannery Row and Carmel, which means this city of 30,000 has ocean proximity without the corresponding price insanity you'd expect on the Central California coast. At a median home value of $692,600 against a median household income of $82,303, the price-to-income ratio lands around 8.4× — steep, but noticeably lower than neighboring Monterey or Pacific Grove, where comparable figures climb far higher. The former Fort Ord, decommissioned in 1994, reshaped the local economy and landscape: California State University, Monterey Bay occupies part of that converted land, and the Veterans Transition Center and Defense Language Institute at nearby Presidio of Monterey keep a significant public-sector and defense employment base within commuting range. The terrain rises gently from sandy flats near the coast into oak-dotted hills, and the Fort Ord National Monument opens thousands of acres of chaparral trails just inland — legitimate backcountry access minutes from subdivisions. Daily highs averaging 65°F year-round with 8.4 hours of sunshine mean fog-cooled mornings and mild afternoons in every season, rarely hot, rarely cold. Rents at $2,314 consume roughly a third of that median income, a ratio that tightens quickly for lower earners in a local economy weighted toward service, education, and government roles rather than high-salary private-sector clusters. Seaside is the part of the Monterey Peninsula where the military-to-university pipeline shaped the street grid more than tourism ever did, and that origin still defines its tradeoffs.
